Silicosis Class Action Settlement

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look at the history and consequences of the Silicosis Class Action Settlement

Unique Selling Point:
Since July news of the largest ever class-action settlement in the history of the gold mining industry has begun permeating the furthest corners of South Africa where thousands of former mine workers have waited for decades, to hear how much their suffering and illness was worth. Around 500,000 breadwinners and their families, hard-hit by silicosis and tuberculosis from working on the mines, were awarded R5 billion collectively in a lawsuit against 14 of the country’s biggest gold mines. Meeting some of the families who have been waiting, Carte Blanche asks whether the victory can change lives.

Press Release:


Since July news of the largest ever class-action settlement in the history of the gold mining industry has begun permeating the furthest corners of South Africa where thousands of former mine workers have waited for decades, to hear how much their suffering and illness was worth. Around 500,000 breadwinners and their families, hard-hit by silicosis and tuberculosis from working on the mines, were awarded R5 billion collectively in a lawsuit against 14 of the country’s biggest gold mines. Meeting some of the families who have been waiting, Carte Blanche asks whether the victory can change lives.

Script:


V/O: On the 26th of July the Gauteng High Court approved the largest class action settlement in South African History

This is the story of how that settlement was reached


CLAIRE LINK: Most of the mineworkers who worked in South Africa’s gold mines came from all over the country in rural areas just like this one in the Eastern Cape. They went to Gauteng to find fortune but instead they found an incurable lung disease called silicosis

BETHWELL: My name is Zama Bethwell Nongubo, I am 71 years old, I worked at Vaal Reefs for 18 years and I have Silicosis

V/O: Silicosis is an irreversible and painful lung disease caused by breathing in massive amounts of silica dust generated though the mining of gold.

The prolonged inhalation of tiny crystalline silica particles results in scarring of the lung tissue, leading to reduced lung function and in the most serious cases, cancer and progressive cystic fibrosis.

Zama Nongubo is just one of an estimated 500 000 mine workers who’ve contracted Silicosis whilst working in South African Gold Mines.

Forced to retire at the age of 47, he has not worked since.




V/O: Zama’s story mirrors that of so many others: a tale of broken dreams and shattered lives with devastating consequences for them and their families.

MAVIS: My name is Mavis Nobukela Wonci, my late husband is Lyndon Nzwabantu, he was working in mines for 17 years. He passed away last year on 3 June 2018. He was diagnosed with Silicosis.






V/O: Lyndon Nzwabantu Wonci was seemingly healthy when he quit working on the mines in 1989.

However, silicosis is a latent and progressive disease. When he returned home, he struggled with his health and contracted Tuberculosis twice.

Then in 2017 he got sick again and was diagnosed with severe silicosis from which he would not recover

V/O: Historically, workers have had very little recourse if they became sick whilst working on the mines as Human Rights Attorney Richard Spoor explains

Richard on the historic injustice that has faced mine workers

V/O: What made matters worse was that workers did not have the right to sue their employers if they fell ill.

V/O: The landmark judgment by the Con Court paved the way for the largest class action in South African history.

It was launched in 2012 against 35 Gold Mines on behalf of thousands of current and former mine workers who contracted Silicosis and TB.

Richard on why class action

A class action as complex as this one saw several law firms collaborating with Richard Spoor’s team, including Carina Du Toit from the Legal Resource Centre

Comments from Carina

V/O: Of the 35 mine companies facing the class action, the 6 largest created the Occupational Lung Disease Working Group, in an effort to form a more collaborative approach in dealing with the matter.

Comment from Michael Murray

V/O: With the Working Group on one side and lawyers representing the workers on the other, the stage was set for years of complex litigation and negotiation

Comments from Richard, Michael & Carina about the negotiation.
V/O: After years of negotiation, a settlement was reached in May 2018.

A minimum amount of R5 billion has been set aside by the 6 mining companies within the Working Group to compensate eligible workers from 1965 to date.

This compensation will be dependent on the degree of the disease

With R70000 for the mildest forms and up to R500 000 for the most serious cases

The settlement also compensates dependents of mine workers who died from Silicosis. They will receive between R70 – R100 thousand in compensation.

V/O: Finally 6 and half years after the Class Action was first filed, the Gauteng High Court in Johannesburg approved the historic settlement in July
V/O: Now that the agreement has been approved, the big question remains: What’s the process for compensation?

Abrie van Vuuren from the working group, explains what will happen next.
